keyVerseText: I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun πτέρνα (ptérna) primarily denotes the heel, referring to the lower part or underside of the foot. Although its precise etymology is uncertain, the word encompasses both the literal heel and related concepts such as the heel-bone, the footstep, or the base of an object, as seen in its use in the Septuagint. This root meaning extends beyond the simple anatomical term to include metaphorical senses involving the lower or foundational part of something, emphasizing position and vulnerability.
usageInScripture: The word πτέρνα appears only once in the New Testament, translated consistently as 'heel.' This singular occurrence in John 13:18 highlights its figurative use, where the heel symbolizes betrayal or opposition. The limited usage underscores the term's specificity and weight, focusing on the concept of one who 'lifts up the heel' against another, a vivid image of treachery rooted in the physical action involving the heel.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding πτέρνα as 'heel' enriches our grasp of biblical imagery concerning human frailty and opposition. The heel, being a vulnerable spot of the body, serves as a powerful metaphor for the place where betrayal and spiritual attack occur. In the Christian faith, this word invites reflection on the reality of betrayal even among close companions, as well as the fulfillment of Scripture through Christ's experience. It reminds believers of the cost of discipleship and the reality of spiritual conflict, while also pointing to Christ's sovereign knowledge and purpose in the midst of such opposition.
keyVerseReflection: In John 13:18, Jesus declares, 'He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me,' using πτέρνα to convey the act of betrayal by one of His own followers. The word 'heel' here intensifies the imagery of treachery, portraying the betrayal as a deliberate and intimate act. This metaphor underscores the fulfillment of Scripture and Jesus’ awareness of the impending betrayal, deepening the reader's appreciation of the gravity and personal nature of Judas's action.
